edges.effect_quant: Hospital-associated disability is common in older adults. A meta-analysis of 7,375 hospitalized adults aged 65 and older estimated a pooled prevalence of new disability of 30% (95% CI 24% to 33%). Cohort studies also show that lower mobility and poorer steadiness during admission strongly track with loss of ADL independence by discharge and follow-up.
edges.population: older adults admitted to acute medical or medical-surgical hospital services, especially those aged 65 years or older
edges.mechanism: Acute illness, bed rest, delirium, sleep disruption, iatrogenic stressors, and low mobility during admission can rapidly decondition older adults and reduce reserve. Even short hospital stays can therefore convert transient illness into durable loss of independence in basic activities of daily living.
edges.summary: This is one of the clearest harmful geriatric systems-level edges. Acute hospital admission is not just a marker of illness severity; it is itself associated with substantial risk of downstream functional decline, particularly when mobility and baseline reserve are poor.
edges.caveats: Hospitalization effects are entangled with the severity of the illness that led to admission, so some measured decline reflects both the acute disease and the hospital process. Even so, the persistence of hospital-associated disability across cohorts and eras makes a genuinely harmful interpretation more credible than a purely confounded one.
